items.question: Which position is long gamma, long vega and short theta?

options.text: A long calendar: sell the 1-month, buy the 3-month
options.why: You gave the calendar positive gamma. It sold the sharper 1-month gamma, so its gamma is negative.
You flipped every sign. A short put is short gamma and short vega, and collects theta.
You took the writer's side. A short call is short gamma and vega, and collects theta.

feedback.correct: A straddle buys movement and pays time decay.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Long gamma and vega means long options.

explain.text: A long straddle has gamma and vega positive and theta negative. A long calendar is long vega but short gamma, and its theta is positive.

items.prose: Same share and strike. Compare the first option's price with the second's. Where a row names a rate, use it; otherwise $r = 0$.
items.question: Type >, = or < in each row.

feedback.correct: Asian and knock-out below, lookback above, American call equal, American put above.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use payoff dominance, then volatility.

byKey.r0c1: An average moves less than a final price, so the Asian is cheaper.
byKey.r1c1: A knock-out pays the vanilla's payoff or nothing.
byKey.r2c1: A lookback pays at least the vanilla on every path.
byKey.r3c1: With no dividend there is no early exercise, so the two are equal.
byKey.r4c1: At 5% an early exercise gains interest on the strike, so the American put is dearer.

explain.text: Dearest first: lookback, vanilla, then the knock-out and the Asian. At 5% the American put is £6.09 against £5.57.

parts.question: The share moves £1.20 in a day. What is the net P&L for 10,000 hedged options?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Gamma gain on the squared move, less one day of theta, times 10,000.

explain.text: Each option nets $0.0459 - 0.0198 = 0.0261$, so £261 for 10,000. Full revaluation gives £255 up and £271 down, since the second-order step is approximate.
